Slightly soluble salt contents in the older terraces Ir02 and Ir15
average 0.08% (n=18) and are therefore not saline, while in the Apb/
ApbBw horizons of Ir02 salt contents can reach 0.16% (slightly saline).
The young terrace soils Ir01 show the lowest salt contents, with only
0.03% (n=19) and Jid-Cs with only 0.02%, and thus in both cases soil
is not saline.
Geochemical results support the premise of a rather homogenous
parent material of soil formation, and in the case of Ir01 and Jid-Cs a
similar weathering intensity and secondary soil formation over the
last two centuries: there is no signiﬁcant vertical alternating of any
element content in the colluvial sediments and soils (Table 4).
The Chemical Index of Alteration (CIA) varies between 57 and 65,
indicating weak silicate weathering (cf. Nesbitt and Young, 1982).
Sediments with ﬂuvial characteristics (Ir01, 13C–15C) and colluvial
material without signs of cultivation and ploughing (Jid-Cs) have a
lower CIA (55 to 58).
3.2. Establishment of natural (NOR) and anthropogenic (137Cs)
radionuclide baseline level
The resulting average mass activity per depth increment of 137Cs,
40K, 226Ra, 232Th are presented in Fig. 6. The different NOR showed an
almost constant vertical distribution of their mass activities (Fig. 6b, c
and d). The natural radioactivity contents of the top soil (0–10 cm)
obtained in the present study (40K=390±4.5 Bq kg−1; 226Ra=24±
0.5 Bq kg−1; 232Th=23±1.2 Bq kg−1) are within the range of back-
ground activity reported for soils worldwide; the world average
concentration levels of 40K, 226Ra and 232Th, in soil being 400 Bq kg−1
with a range of 140 to 850, 35 Bq kg−1 with a range of 17 to 60, and
30 Bq kg−1 with a range of 11 to 64, respectively (UNSCEAR, 2000).
Based on NOR information, the Raeq reached 84±6 Bq kg−1,
and the external gamma dose rate of the top soils in terrace Jid-Cs
(0–10 cm) was estimated at 41±3 nGy h−1 (n=10), 28% lower than
the world average of 57 nGy h−1 (UNSCEAR, 2000). The contribution
of 40K, 232Th and 226Ra to the external dose rate in this upper terrace
soil Jid-Cs is 40%, 34% and 27% respectively.
As expected, the 137Cs soil activity of the undisturbed top terrace
(pasture) shows an exponential vertical decrease with almost no
signiﬁcant detectable 137Cs below 20 cm (cf. Fig. 6). In terms of areal
activity (Bq m−2), 80% of the 137Cs is concentred in the top 10 cm
and 98% in the ﬁrst 20 cm. Based on the ten soil proﬁles collected
(0–40 cm) the estimated population mean of 137Cs baseline inventory
was established at 3440±820 Bq m−2 (mean±2SE; CV=38%). This
value, which is in the same order of magnitude as the average median
CVs of undisturbed sites of 5 to 41% (Owens and Walling, 1996;
Sutherland, 1991, 1996), will be used as the 137Cs base-line level for
future assessments of soil erosion and redistribution rates for the
terrace soils situated below Jid-Cs (cf. Fig. 3).

4.1. Agricultural suitability and vulnerability to degradation of Yemeni

agricultural suitability of accumulated materials and the vulnerability

terraces, the composition of the colluvial material accumulated in

a depth of 60–115 cm (King et al., 1983). Therefore, independent of

and even relocation processes take place below the ploughing zone
while being farmed. Aside from silicate weathering, CaCO3 enrich-

4.2. Assessment of ancient and modern erosion by radiometric data
To estimate soil erosion in ancient times and to proof the
applicability of radionuclids with the aim of assessing the vulnerabil-
ity of terraces to degradation, the combination of two methods have
been applied: 14C for ancient erosion and FRN for modern erosion
over the last 50 years, whereby the FRN study at this stage aimed
ﬁrst to establish a NOR and 137Cs base-line level of an undisturbed
terraced site in Wadi Al-Jidar.
Three sites have been 14C dated: IR01, Ir02 and Ir16. Terrace Ir16, a
badly destroyed terrace yields a buried humus-rich soil with an age of
2670–2470 cal yr BC (cf. Table 3). This age of the humic acid indicates
that the terraced slope was cultivated from the 3rd millennium BC.
The oldest AMS 14C dated charcoal was found in the colluvial layer in
proﬁle Ir02 (7C1 horizon); the maximum age of colluvial deposition
there is 560–380 cal yr BC, and the charcoal fragment at 235–260 cm
depth (3C horizon) has an age of 940–1020 cal yr AD. Thus, soils
situated above are a product of cultivation within the last 1000 years.
Also interesting is the estimated rate of material accumulation: 4 m of
suspended silty sediments have been accumulated gradually behind
the terrace wall over a period of 2000 years (cf. Fig. 4).
In contrast, and in consideration of the high number of layers (14),
their shallowness and their higher sand contents, the young terrace
Ir01 is assumed to be mainly a product of the 18th to 20th century
AD: roughly estimated, at least 2 m of deposit were accumulated
during the last 200 years (cf. Fig. 4): the charcoal having ages of
1670–1780 cal yr AD and 1870–1920 AD.
Taking the study of Brakenridge (1985) into account, who already
used 14C dating to estimate erosion rates, it is obvious that bedrock
erosion and lateral erosion was, at 1 m per 100 yr, much lower in
ancient times (in his study the Early Holocene) than in modern times at
1.3 m per century. Although Tennessee is not comparable to the Yemen
Highlands – regarding time scale, geology, precipitation and discharge –
it is evident, that heavy episodic precipitation occurring in the Late
Holocene increases erosion, in contrast to ancient times. As the climate
in Yemen became drier during the Late Holocene, precipitation events
turned episodic and the discharge behaviour of wadi ﬂoods was
modiﬁed (Wilkinson, 2005). In these geomorphodynamic unstable
phases, modern erosion in the Yemen Highlands was and is additionally
intensiﬁed due to the abandonment of terraces.
Since it is not possible to calculate modern erosion rates over the
last 50 years by using radiocarbon dating, a set of complementary
radiometric methods was chosen, which involve the establishment of
the NOR and 137Cs base-line level for soils in the area of Tertiary
basalt. The paper of Abd El-Mageed et al. (2011) provides very
informative activity levels of NOR and
137Cs in Yemeni top soils
(0–2 cm, n=16) in the area of Juban town, although developed on
sandstone substratum. The average radioactivity concentrations of 40K,
226Ra and 232Th in the 16 top soils analysed are 822, 44, 58 Bq kg−1,
respectively, and the
137Cs mass activity content ranges from 4.8
to 23.2 Bq kg−1 (Abd El-Mageed et al., 2011). The mean activity
NOR's concentration in our study is lower than these values. In fact, the
226Ra/232Th around 1 as well as the relative low natural radioactivity
measured in the Wadi Al-Jidar terraces versus the values of Abd El-
Mageed et al. (2011) are typical for basalt material (Eisenbud and
Gesell, 1997).
As Chernobyl fallout did not signiﬁcantly affect the Middle East
region (FAO, 1989), the anthropogenic deposit of 137Cs in the area
(n=10; 3440 Bq m−2) is representative of the various nuclear
weapon test releases that took place during the 1950s and the
1960s. The background level of 137Cs measured could also be very
useful in the future to assess the potential magnitude of any new
release from a Nuclear Power Plant accident that could affect the
Yemeni territory. According to FAO (1989) the approximate relative
contributions of anthropogenic radionuclides (fallout from nuclear
weapons testing) to the average annual effective dose equivalent
represents only 1% of the total exposure. So, in uncontaminated area
the contribution of radio-cesium to the total exposure should be
negligible. The assessment of external dose rate for 137Cs using the
speciﬁc dose rate conversion factors of 0.11761 for the top soil radio-
cesium content proposed by Mabit et al. (2012) can be established at
2.6 nGy h−1. Taking into account the full soil proﬁle (0–40 cm), a
similar value of 2.3±0.5 nGy h−1 using the Radioecological Software
Package (cf. Velasco et al., 2004) has been evaluated. In both tested
case, as expected the contribution of 137Cs to the external gamma
dose rate is negligible reaching only 6 to 7% of the dose rate produced
by the NOR.
In the highlands of Yemen, evidence of wind erosion and eolian
deposit from local sources (e.g. Nettleton and Chadwick, 1996) and
the Ramlat As-Sabatayn (cf. Fig. 1) can be found. In the frame of
further investigations, the current set-up of the NOR, Raeq and D
values of the upper terrace Jid-Cs will allow the assessment and
comparison of the potential impact of loess deposit in the catchment
area of Wadi Hawar.
Soil physical and chemical data, estimation of erosion in ancient
terraces using 14C, the determination of NOR and 137Cs base-line
levels in the undisturbed highest terraced soils of Wadi Al-Jidar/Eryan
appears to be a promising complementary and integrative approach
for future assessments of soil erosion magnitudes in the highly
degraded tropical Yemen Highlands.
